title: How to organize windows on Mac with Stage Manager: a guide for developers in 2026
metaTitle: Organize Windows on Mac with Stage Manager: Developer Guide
description: Organize windows on Mac with Stage Manager, Split View and Mission Control. Free fixes for developers with a cluttered desktop, plus where Lazur helps.
targetKeyword: how to organize windows on mac with stage manager
intro: To organize windows on Mac with Stage Manager, turn it on in Control Center and drag the apps you use together into one group. Stage Manager keeps recent apps on the left and the active group in the center, so you stop searching the whole screen. Split View, Mission Control, and a free app called Rectangle fill the gaps that Stage Manager leaves.
tldr: Turn on Stage Manager in Control Center, then drag apps into the center to build a group.
Close finished windows with ⌘W. Minimizing only sends them to the Dock.
Use Split View for two windows side by side. Use Mission Control (⌃↑) to see every window at once.
Rectangle is a free app for snapping windows with shortcuts. Lazur can point at controls and guide you, but it does not move windows for you.

blocks.text: Why your Mac desktop fills up so fast

Windows pile up because closing one takes a decision, and leaving it open takes nothing. A code editor, a browser full of docs, a terminal, Slack, and a ticket tracker can each carry several windows. Mac keeps all of them alive. The desktop looks busy long before it looks broken.
Clutter costs you in small searches. Your eyes scan the Dock, the ⌘Tab switcher, and the stacks of windows behind each other. Each search is quick. Across a workday, they add up and break your focus.
Start with a window audit
Before you change any setting, look at what you have. Press ⌃↑ to open Mission Control. Every open window appears in one layer, so you can see the full mess at once. Click any window to jump to it.

items: Open Mission Control with ⌃↑, or swipe up with three fingers on the trackpad.
Sort windows into piles: working now, needed today, and finished.
Close each finished window with ⌘W. The app can keep running, which is what you want.
Move the windows you need today into a Stage Manager group or a Space.
Leave the rest in Mission Control, where you can find them later.

blocks.title: Close, don't minimize
blocks.text: Minimizing sends a window into the Dock, where it still sits in your head. Closing it with ⌘W clears the space. Use ⌘Q only when you have finished with the whole app, because it quits every window in that app.
Stage Manager on Mac: turning it on and building groups

Stage Manager puts your current work in the center and lines recently used apps up along the left side. Click a recent app on the left and it moves to the center. Apple describes it as a way to keep your desktop organized around the apps you use now.

To turn it on, open Control Center in the menu bar and switch on Stage Manager. You can also open System Settings > Desktop & Dock and set it there. Apple says Stage Manager stays available in Control Center and can be added to the menu bar.

blocks.title: If Stage Manager will not turn on
blocks.text: Open System Settings > Desktop & Dock and check the Mission Control settings. Turn on 'Displays have separate Spaces', then switch Stage Manager on again. Apple's help page lists this as the fix when Stage Manager will not start.
To build a group, drag an app into the center. Apple says dragging an app there adds it to a group. Switch groups by clicking one on the left, and all of its apps come back to the center together.

items: Open Cursor or VS Code and drag it into the center.
Drag the Chrome window with your docs into the center beside it. Stage Manager adds it to the same group.
Open Slack and look at the left side. Recent apps show up there, so you can click Slack when a thread needs you.
Keep the editor and docs in the center while you work. Chat and tickets wait on the left.

blocks.text: Groups work best when each one has a single job. A group that holds the editor, the docs, the terminal, and chat is just a new pile of windows. Split your groups by task, not by app type.
Split View on Mac for code and docs

Split View puts two app windows side by side, each taking half the screen. It suits the common developer pair: an editor on one side and a browser with docs on the other. Hover over the green button in the window's top left corner, then choose Left of Screen or Right of Screen.
You can also set it up from Mission Control. Drag a window onto the thumbnail of a full-screen app in the Spaces bar, then click that thumbnail. Apple's Mission Control page describes this route.

Full-screen mode has one catch. It hides the menu bar until the pointer moves to the top of the screen. If you forget, you will hunt for menus that are not there. Move the pointer up and the bar comes back.

blocks.title: Stage Manager and Split View together
blocks.text: Some third-party sites say these two cannot run side by side. The Apple help pages do not say that. Test it on your own Mac, with your own apps, before you rely on it.
Mission Control and Spaces when the desktop is full

Mission Control is the overview. It shows every open window and every Space in one view. A Space is a separate desktop. A full-screen app gets its own Space, which keeps it out of your way until you visit it.
Use Spaces to split big areas of work. Keep one project in one Space and chat in another. On the default setup, ⌃← and ⌃→ move you between Spaces. You can change these shortcuts in System Settings.
Stage Manager is for working. Mission Control is for finding. Use each one for its job, and the desktop stays readable.
Rectangle as a free window snapper

Apple's tools cover most cases, but some developers want faster snapping. Rectangle is a free, open-source app that moves and resizes windows with keyboard shortcuts or snap areas. Its website says it supports macOS 14 or later.

Rectangle Pro is the paid upgrade. It adds faster snapping and custom shortcuts, and it has a 10-day free trial. One Pro license can be active on 3 devices at a time. Check Rectangle's site for current pricing.

Pick one main tool. Stage Manager and Rectangle both move windows, and running both can feel like two people rearranging the same desk. Try each for a few days, then keep the one that stays out of your way.
A worked example for an afternoon of code, docs, and chat

Say you are fixing a bug in an API client. Cursor holds the code. Chrome holds the vendor docs and a staging dashboard. Slack has a thread from QA, and Linear shows the ticket. That is a handful of apps, and most of them have several windows each.

items: Turn on Stage Manager and drag Cursor into the center. That becomes your coding group.
Drag the docs window into the center beside Cursor. Both now sit in one group.
When you need to read docs next to a long file, use Split View on the docs window. Hover the green button and choose a side.
Keep Slack and Linear on the left. Click them only when a thread or ticket needs you.
When the fix ships, close the docs window with ⌘W instead of minimizing it.

blocks.text: Notice what this avoids. You do not need every window on screen while you type. The docs appear when you need them, and chat waits on the left. If you swap Cursor for VS Code, the steps stay the same.
Xcode and iOS simulators open their own windows. When one seems to vanish, check Mission Control before you start hunting. The window is often in another Space or behind a full-screen app.

blocks.text: Mistakes that bring the clutter back

items: Minimizing windows you will never reopen. They still sit in the Dock and in your head.
Leaving full-screen apps in Spaces you never visit. They wait there, and you forget them.
Putting every app in one Stage Manager group. A group needs a single job to be useful.
Pressing ⌘Q when you meant ⌘W. Quit removes every window of that app at once.
Skipping the reset. Clutter returns after every busy week, so clear it on a set day.

blocks.text: Clutter also feeds on interruptions. Each switch leaves part of your attention on the last task. Sophie Leroy's 2009 paper in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes is titled around this effect, which it calls attention residue. For a routine that helps after switches, read [how to recover focus after interruptions while coding](/for/developers/problems/developer-context-switching-recovery-time).
What the Microsoft numbers do and do not tell you

Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index reports that 80% of the global workforce says it lacks the time or energy to do its job. It also says employees are interrupted by a meeting, email, or ping every 2 minutes on average. Those figures come from one company's survey and data. They do not prove that window clutter causes either problem.
This guide does not cite a verified figure for the minutes that clutter costs each day. We could not find a primary source for one. Treat any number you see for it with caution.
Where Lazur helps with window setup

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥⌘ and ask a question, and Lazur answers out loud. It looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored.

Ask where something is and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen. Ask how to do something and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. You do the clicking. Lazur does not click buttons, move windows, or operate other apps for you.

Lazur is not a window manager, and it is not a plugin for Cursor, Slack, or any other app. It explains what is on screen, points at controls, and drafts and types text when you ask. Hold fn to dictate clean text at the cursor in any app.

If your windows show customer data, patient records, or client files, follow your employer's rules before you ask Lazur about the screen. Your employer's policy comes first, even when a tool makes the task faster.
Next steps for your desktop

Start with the audit and one Stage Manager group. Give it a week. Then decide whether you need Split View, Spaces, or Rectangle. If you live in Cursor, our [Cursor page for developers](/for/developers/cursor) covers the app's own shortcuts. See [Lazur pricing](/pricing) for the current trial and plans, or [download the app](/download) to try it on your Mac.

faq.question: Can I use Stage Manager and Split View together?
faq.answer: Apple's help pages describe both features, and they do not say the two conflict. Some third-party sites claim they cannot run together. Test it on your own Mac with your own apps before you rely on either one.

faq.question: Why is Stage Manager missing from Control Center?
faq.answer: Open System Settings > Desktop & Dock and check the Mission Control settings. If Stage Manager will not turn on, enable 'Displays have separate Spaces', then try again. Apple's help page gives this as the fix.

faq.question: Which macOS version do these menu paths match?
faq.answer: Apple's Stage Manager page reflects macOS 27. Apple's manage windows page lists macOS Tahoe 26 and macOS Sequoia 15. Menu names can change between versions, so check your version under Apple menu > About This Mac.

faq.question: Is Rectangle free?
faq.answer: Yes, the base app is free and open source, and it supports macOS 14 or later. Rectangle Pro is a paid upgrade with a 10-day free trial. One Pro license covers 3 devices at a time.

faq.question: Does Lazur move my windows for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It points at controls, answers out loud, and guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available. Check the download page for the current platform details.

faq.question: Is my screen sent anywhere when I use Lazur?
faq.answer: Lazur looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: What if I cannot find a window at all?
faq.answer: Open Mission Control with ⌃↑ and look for it there. If the app is running but you see no window, switch to it with ⌘Tab and check its Window menu. The window may sit in another Space.

costs.title: Time lost hunting for windows
costs.text: Every search for a window is small friction. You scan the Dock, the ⌘Tab switcher, and stacked windows, then guess again when the first guess is wrong. This guide does not put a number on the minutes lost, because we could not verify one. Track a normal afternoon for a week if you want your own figure.

costs.title: Attention that stays on the last task
costs.text: Switching away from a window does not clear your head at once. Part of your attention stays with what you left. Sophie Leroy's 2009 paper describes this as attention residue. Clutter multiplies the switches, and every switch leaves a little residue behind.

costs.title: Work pressure that already exists
costs.text: Microsoft's 2025 survey found that 80% of the global workforce says it lacks the time or energy to do its job. Clutter does not cause that alone. A cluttered desktop can make a tight day feel tighter, and that is the part you can fix.

costs.title: Messages that sit unread
costs.text: A Slack window you never look at can hide a question from a teammate for hours. Stage Manager shows recent apps on the left, so chat stays easy to reach. Pick fixed times to check chat, and keep it in the same place.

costs.title: Mistakes in the wrong window
costs.text: When many windows overlap, it is easy to type a command in the wrong terminal or paste a secret into the wrong chat. A clean layout lowers that risk. Before you run a command that changes data, check the window title and the app name in the menu bar.

causes.title: Closing takes a decision, opening takes none
causes.text: Leaving a window open is the default. Closing it means you decided it is finished. macOS also keeps an app running after you close its last window, so the app stays in the Dock and the mess stays on screen. Most people never choose to clear windows, so they build up.

causes.title: Apps open windows faster than you close them
causes.text: Browsers, editors, and chat apps open new windows for every link, file, or thread. Each one looks important when it opens. A single afternoon can leave you with a pile that you never planned.

causes.title: Full-screen apps and extra Spaces hide the pile
causes.text: A full-screen app moves to its own Space. Out of sight, it gets forgotten. Then the Space turns into storage, and you return to it only when something breaks. Hidden windows still count as clutter when you need them.

causes.title: Minimizing moves the pile to the Dock
causes.text: Minimize feels tidy, but the window stays in the Dock. The Dock becomes a row of thumbnails you have to read. Over time, the Dock fills with the same kind of clutter as the desktop.

causes.title: Interruptions force constant switching
causes.text: Microsoft reports that employees are interrupted by a meeting, email, or ping every 2 minutes on average. Each interruption sends you to another window. You then return to your work and look for it again. More interruptions usually mean more windows open at once.

causes.title: Default macOS gives you no grouping
causes.text: Without a grouping tool, every window looks equally important. Stage Manager, Spaces, and Split View add structure, but you need to set them up before they help. This page shows how to add that structure with tools that come with macOS.

fixes.title: Build one Stage Manager group per job
fixes.text: Turn on Stage Manager in Control Center. Drag the apps for one job into the center, such as the editor and the docs. Keep chat and tickets on the left. Start with one group, and add a second only when the first feels crowded. This costs nothing and uses the built-in apps.

fixes.title: Use Split View for two windows at a time
fixes.text: Hover over the green button, then choose Left of Screen or Right of Screen. Use it for code next to docs, or for a log next to the file you are fixing. Full-screen mode hides the menu bar, so move the pointer to the top when you need a menu.

fixes.title: Find lost windows with Mission Control
fixes.text: Press ⌃↑ to see every window in one layer. Click a window to jump to it. Then press ⌘W to close it once you are on it. Mission Control is the fastest way to audit a desktop that has grown messy over a week.

fixes.title: Give each project its own Space
fixes.text: Add desktops from the Spaces bar at the top of Mission Control. Keep one project in one Space. Move between Spaces with ⌃← and ⌃→. A project Space holds the editor, the docs, and the terminal, so you return to a clean desktop each time.

fixes.title: Close windows before you minimize them
fixes.text: Close finished windows with ⌘W, and keep the app running if you need it later. Quit the whole app with ⌘Q only when you are done for the day. This habit removes the window instead of storing it somewhere you will forget.

fixes.title: Try Rectangle for keyboard snapping
fixes.text: Rectangle is free and open source. It moves and resizes windows with keyboard shortcuts or snap areas, and it supports macOS 14 or later. Use the free version first. Upgrade to Rectangle Pro only if you need faster snapping or custom shortcuts.

fixes.title: Clear the desktop on a set day
fixes.text: Pick one time each week to clear windows. On that day, close finished windows, check the Dock, and tidy the Spaces bar. A short block often works better than a big cleanup you keep putting off.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Audit every open window
plan.text: Open Mission Control with ⌃↑ and read what you see. Close every window you finished with ⌘W. Note which apps you need today. Leave the rest for later.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Turn on Stage Manager and make one group
plan.text: Turn it on in Control Center. Drag your editor and the browser with docs into the center. Use only that group for the morning. Notice what you still reach for on the left side.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Try Split View for reading
plan.text: Use Split View when you read a long doc beside code. Hover the green button and choose a side. Full-screen apps hide the menu bar, so move the pointer to the top when you need menus.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Set up Spaces for projects
plan.text: Keep one project per Space. Put chat and email in a separate Space. Move between Spaces with ⌃← and ⌃→. Use Mission Control to check where a window went.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Decide on snapping and clear out
plan.text: If Split View feels slow, try Rectangle's free shortcuts for a few days. Then pick one main tool. Close finished windows, check the Dock, and reset the desktop before you leave.
